parole.significato: Used to form abstract nouns from verbs, adjectives or other nouns
parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *-iþō. Cognate with English -th.

parole.significato: Used to form nouns from verbs
parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *-þiz. Cognate with English -t.

parole.significato: forms agent nouns and instrument nouns such as tools
parole.testo: From Old Swedish -il, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *-ilaz. Cognate with English -le, -el.

parole.significato: -ing; added to verbs that do not end with an unstressed -a to form the present participle
parole.testo: From Proto-Germanic *-andz.

parole.significato: -ess; makes a female version of a title, often referring to the bearer's wife
parole.testo: From Old Swedish -inna, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *-inī.

parole.significato: European perch, redfin perch, English perch, Perca fluviatilis
parole.testo: From Old Swedish aghborre, aborre, from a combination of Proto-Germanic *agjō (whence also egg) and Proto-Germanic *burzô (whence Swedish borre), which is related to Swedish borste and English burr. Cognate with Danish aborre, Norwegian Bokmål abbor, Norwegian Nynorsk åbor, Faroese áburra, Icelandic
Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *arô.

parole.significato: an ark, a box; the Ark of the Covenant
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ark, from late Proto-Germanic *arkō, borrowed from Latin arca in pre-Christian times.
From Old Swedish bī, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bi (“by”). Cognate to English by.

parole.significato: barley, particularly of the genus Hordeum
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish biug, biugh, biog, from Proto-Germanic *bewwą.

parole.significato: to burn, to be on fire
parole.testo: From Old Swedish brinna, from Proto-Germanic *brinnaną.

parole.significato: a board (long, relatively thin piece of wood – compare planka)
parole.testo: From a surface analysis, feminine form of bräde (compare Norwegian Nynorsk bræde m, bræda f), from Old Swedish brædha, suggesting an earlier form akin to *bræða, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bredą (“board, plank, shelf”), an e-grade byform of *burdą (“board, plank”), Swedish bord. Presumably from

parole.significato: the board of a board game
parole.testo: From a surface analysis, masculine form of bräda (compare Norwegian Nynorsk bræde m, bræda f), from Old Swedish brædha, suggesting an earlier form of *bræði, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bredą (“board, plank, shelf”), an e-grade byform of *burdą (“board, plank”), Swedish bord. Presumably from Mid

parole.significato: to make unpleasant noise (often of rumbling, like from a car or machinery, or thunder)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish buldra. Arguably from Proto-Germanic *bellaną (“to roar”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel-. Arguably onomatopoeic. Possibly related to Dutch bulderen, German poltern, German bollern.

parole.significato: document granting the right to pursue certain professions, license, work permit
parole.testo: bur (“burgher”) + brev (“letter”). The word bur was used in the meaning "burgher" or "city inhabitant", but could also mean "villager", "farmer", or "neighbor". From Proto-Germanic *būraz. Related to German Bauer and Dutch boer. See also burskap.
From Old Swedish böra, from Old Norse byrja (“to befit”), from Proto-Germanic *gaburjaną.
Probably from Proto-Germanic *dangijaną with original meaning "strike lightly and often". Doublet of dingla and dänga.

parole.significato: suck, suckle; milk from the mother (human or animal) directly to the offspring
parole.testo: From dia (“to suckle”), from Proto-Germanic *dijōną (“to suckle”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suckle”). Related to dägga (däggdjur).
Inherited from Old Swedish di, dia, from Proto-Germanic *dijōną, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck, suckle”).

From dangla. Probably from Proto-Germanic *dangijaną with original meaning "strike lightly and often". Doublet of dänga. Compare Icelandic dingla, Danish dingle, English dingle-dangle. See also tingeltangel.

parole.significato: clean (seeds and grains) from chaff and husks by shaking
parole.testo: From Proto-Germanic *drupatjaną. Doublet of drypa. Modern sense of "debate" coined by Viktor Rydberg and Sven Adolf Hedlund during the latter half of the 19th century.

parole.significato: a short, roughly cylindrical protrusion to prevent slipping (on ice)
parole.testo: Ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *dubilaz (“dowel, peg”), presumably via Middle Low German. Compare German Dübel (“dowel”).

parole.significato: a grove; a smallish collection of trees
parole.testo: Probably to Proto-Germanic *dungō? Related to dynga, Old Swedish dyngia, Old Norse dyngja.

From Old Swedish ællæghis, from Proto-Germanic *aljas (genitive of *aljaz), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élyos. Adjective sense 1 might derive from adverb sense 2, which is also intuitively what it means. Cognate with English else.
From Old Swedish ællivu, from Proto-Germanic *ainalif, a compound of *ainaz and *-lif. Compare Norwegian and Danish elleve, Icelandic ellefu and Faroese ellivu.

parole.significato: male pig used for breeding purposes
parole.testo: From Old Swedish fargalter. The first element far- is from Proto-Germanic *farhaz, from Proto-Indo-European *pórḱos, cognate to English farrow. The second element is equivalent of modern Swedish galt (“boar, male pig”).

parole.significato: to grin (smile in a cheeky, mocking, silly, stupid, or similar way, or "in a less beautiful way," as Svensk ordbok puts…
parole.testo: From Proto-Germanic *flinōną (“to bare (one's teeth), smile”), from a Proto-Indo-European *pley- (“bare, bald, flat”). Cognate with Elfdalian flinå (“smile”); outside of Germanic, compare Lithuanian pli̇̀kas (“bald”), Latvian pliks (“bare, bald”). The root may be further connected to Proto-Indo-Euro

parole.significato: to steer (a young person) towards desirable behavior or greater personal development (to foster desirable things), to r…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish fostra, derived from Proto-Germanic *fōstrą. Cognate of English foster.

The current form ending in -ande (normally indicating a present participle) was used already in Old Swedish, but the more original form främmad lives on in spoken dialects in Götaland (including Närke) and is sometimes used in written poetry. Traces back to Old Saxon fremithi and Old High German fra

From Old Swedish frān, extended (with unexplained -n) from older Old Swedish frā (compare the archaic/dialectal alternative form frå), a proclitic form of Old Swedish fram, from Proto-Germanic *fram (“from”), from Proto-Germanic *promo- (“forth, forward”).
From Old Swedish fynd, from Proto-Germanic *fundiz. Related to finna (“to find”).

From Old Swedish fiurir, fiūri, fȳrir, fȳri, from Runic East Norse ᚠᛁᚢᚱᛁᛦ (fiuriʀ) (Old West Norse fjórir), from Proto-Germanic *fedwōr, from *kʷetwṓr, the neuter form of Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres.
fyra + -faldig, from Old Swedish fyrafalder, from Proto-Germanic *feþurfalþaz.
Inherited from Old Swedish fang. First attested in the 13th century. Doublet of få (“receive”) and fånga (“catch”): all from Proto-Germanic *fanhaną (“to capture”).
Partly from Old Swedish for, Proto-Germanic *furai. Partly from Old Swedish fyrir, firi, fyre, from Old Norse fyrir, from Proto-Germanic *furi.

parole.significato: to whinge, to whine, to nag, to complain incessantly about minor issues
parole.testo: Unknown. Arguably onomatopoeic. Arguably related to Proto-Germanic *gnīdaną (“to rub”). Compare Danish gnælde, Icelandic gnella (“to scream”), Norwegian Nynorsk gnella, Old Norse gnǫllra (“to howl, to bark”).
From Proto-Germanic *grabōną, related to English grab; see there for more. Attested since 1651.

parole.significato: grit (personal trait; in the expression gott gry), courage, spirit
parole.testo: Related to gryt, gryta, and English grit, all from Proto-Germanic *greutą.
Probably from Proto-Germanic *gutjōn, related to *geutaną (“to pour”).

parole.significato: pool; lagoon; a small, swampy pond, lake, or other body of standing water. For example, the shallow, still-standing wat…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish *gyl, from Proto-Germanic *guljō, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeyh₁- (“to gape, yawn”), same source as Proto-Germanic *gīnaną. Unrelated to Turkish göl.
From Old Swedish harmber, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *harmaz. Cognate with English harm.
From Old Swedish hungrogher, from Proto-Germanic *hungrugaz.
Shortened form of huru, from Old Swedish hwaru, from neuter dative of Proto-Germanic *hwar

parole.significato: dog command for calling off and silencing (driving) dogs en pursuit
parole.testo: Of imitative origin. Originally a call to stop, chase away, or silence dogs. The noun is attested since 1645, but the root appears earlier in Old Swedish huta (verb). The cognates Middle High German hiuzen, hūzen (“to call to pursuit”) suggests a potential Pan-Germanic forefather, likely involving d

parole.significato: to breed, to nest (breed and raise offspring, of birds)
parole.testo: From Proto-Germanic *hakjaną. Cognate with English hatch, German hecken.
From Old Swedish høster, Old Norse haustr m, from Proto-Germanic *harbustaz, *harbistaz. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kerp-.

From Old Swedish edizla, idhisla. The first part of the word is derived from the Old Swedish particle ið- denoting a repeated action also found in eda and idra, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *idi, and cognate to English ed- (cf. eddish). The second part of the word is a derivation of the equivalent
From Old Swedish īghulkutter, from īghul (“hedgehog”) + the root of Swedish kotte (“rounded object”). The first element is from Proto-Germanic *igilaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eǵʰis (“hedgehog”).
Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *eutaz (“Jute”). Compare Old Norse jótar.

parole.significato: omen (usually in the more literal sense)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish iærtekn, iærtighne. Uncertain origin. The first half of compound probably from Proto-Germanic *erknaz and related to Gothic 𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌺𐌽𐍃 (airkns) and Middle High German erchan. Cognate of Icelandic jarteikn, Danish jærtegn.
Inherited from Old Swedish kif, from Proto-Germanic *kībaną.

parole.significato: a chunk (of material, often wood or metal)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Germanic *klumpô. Cognate with Latin globus. Doublet of klabb, klimp, and klump.
From Proto-Germanic *klinganą. Cognate of English cling. Compare origin of Danish klynge (“cluster”) and German Klüngel (“clique”). Doublet of klänga.

parole.significato: a crotch (the area where something branches, in particular a branch from a tree trunk)
parole.testo: From Proto-Germanic *klukjaną, from *klu- (“to ball up, conglomerate, amass”), from Proto-Indo-European *glew- (“to ball up; lump, mass”).
Compare Icelandic kleggi, English clag (“glue or paste”). From Proto-Germanic *klajjô (“clay”), from Proto-Indo-European *gleh₁y- (“to stick together”). Doublet of kli, klister, and kläde.

parole.significato: to knock; to rap one's knuckles against something, e.g. against a door
parole.testo: Probably ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *knukōną (“to knock”). Compare Dutch knakken, German knacken.
From Proto-Germanic *knuzlijaną (“to beat; push; mash”), from Proto-Indo-European *gen- (“to squeeze, pinch, kink, ball up”). Compare German knallen, Dutch knallen and Danish knalde.

parole.significato: a low, rocky, rounded islet (skerry) (in a coastal archipelago)
parole.testo: Related to kubbe (“sawed-off tree trunk”) and Old Norse kúfóttr, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *kuppaz (“hilltop, knoll”).
Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *kulþa, *kulþō, variants of *kelþaz (“fetus”).

parole.significato: to twitter (make high-pitched vocalizations typical of (smaller) birds)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish qvitra. Compare Danish kvidre, German zwitschern. Arguably from Proto-Germanic *twitwizōną.

parole.significato: to suffocate, to asphyxiate; to cause someone to suffer severely reduced oxygen supply to their body
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kvæfia, qvæfia, (compare Old Icelandic kvefja, kefja), from Proto-Germanic *kwēbijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷeh₂bʰ- (“to dive, dive in”). Cognate with Old Norse kœfa, kvæfa, Icelandic kæfa.

parole.significato: character, nature, disposition (of a person or animal or group)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish kynne. Arguably from Proto-Germanic *kundaz (“born; of a particular disposition”), compare with origin of kön. Otherwise possibly related to kunna (from Proto-Germanic *kunnaną).

parole.significato: to lap (take up (liquid) with the tongue)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish lapa, from Proto-Germanic *lappōną, from Proto-Indo-European *leb-. Doublet of läppja.

parole.significato: a load (amount transported at one time (on a cart, (open) trailer, or the like, or carried), also as an (informal) unit…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish las. Originally the past participle of a verb derived from Proto-Germanic *hlaþaną (“to load”). Doublet of lada and last.
By surface analysis, lass + -a. Cognate of Danish læsse. Originally from Proto-Germanic *hlaþaną. Doublet of ladda and lasta.
From Proto-Germanic *hlīþrō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱléy-treh₂ (“shelter, covering”), from *ḱley- (“to shelter, cover”) + *-treh₂. Compare Gothic 𐌷𐌻𐌴𐌹𐌸𐍂𐌰 (hleiþra, “hull, tent”).
From Old Swedish loppa, from Proto-Germanic *luppōn-, which could be related to *hlaupaną (“to leap, jump”), see also German lüpfen.

From dialectal Swedish lubber (“fat and sluggish person”), from Proto-Germanic *lubbǭ (“that which hangs or dangles”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewbʰ-, *lep- (“to peel, skin”). See also English lubber, English lob, Danish lobbes (“bumpkin, clown”).

parole.significato: loin (the flesh above the hip bone)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish länd, from Proto-Germanic *landį̄. Cognate with Danish lænd, Norwegian lend, Icelandic lend, German Lende, English lend, possibly related to Latin lumbus.

parole.significato: to sip (drink slowly, small mouthfuls at a time)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish læpia, from Proto-Germanic *lapjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *leb-. Doublet of lapa.
Probably inherited from Proto-Germanic *maitaną.
Likely from Proto-Germanic *mūk-. Cognate with Dutch muik (“secret attack”).

Derived from Proto-Germanic *malaną (“to grind”). Shift in sense from "that which has been ground or milled", to "floury". Doublet of mjöl and mala. Cognate of Icelandic mjalli and mjöll. Arguably related to Mjölner.

parole.significato: an amount; a quantity or a volume
parole.testo: Derived from Proto-Germanic *managiþō, possibly through Danish mængde. Compare Norwegian Nynorsk mengd.

parole.significato: a hub (central part of a wheel)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish navan, cognate with English nave, both from Proto-Germanic *nabō.

parole.significato: to pick (usually pills from the surface of a textile, or eyebrows), (of eyebrows) to pluck
parole.testo: Disputed. Possibly inherited from Proto-Germanic *hnuppōną (“tear off”). Possibly verbification of the noun. Compare origin of nypa.
Inherited from Old Swedish nor, from Proto-Germanic *narwaz. Cognate with English narrow.

parole.significato: to use, to make use of for benefit
parole.testo: Related to nytta (“benefit”), njuta. From Old Swedish nytia, from Proto-Germanic *nutjōną
From Proto-Germanic *nasją (“foothill; headland, cape”). Cognate with English ness; etymologically connected with nose.
From Old Swedish okra, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *wōkraz. Compare German wuchern and Dutch woekeren.
From Old Swedish orff, Old Norse orf, from Proto-Germanic *wurba-, related to *warpą.
From Proto-Germanic *prattuz. Compare Dutch praat and English prate.
Inherited from Old Swedish risi, from Proto-Germanic *risiz. Cognate of Danish rise, Icelandic risi, Dutch reus, German Riese.

parole.significato: ray (marine fish with a flat body, large wing-like fins, and a whip-like tail)
parole.testo: Possibly ultimately from Proto-Germanic *rūhwaz (“rough”), referring to the fish's texture. See also Middle Low German roche, ruche, Middle Dutch roche, rogghe, Danish rokke.

Related to ruse. Perhaps from Proto-Germanic *hurskijaną (“to startle, drive”), from *hurskaz (“fast, rapid, quick”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run, hurry”). Cognate with Old High German hurscan (“to speed, accelerate”), Old English horsc (“quick, quick-witted, clever”). Possibly cognate
Inherited from Old Swedish ræfst (“punishment”), from Proto-Germanic *rafsijaną (“to punish”). Cognate of Icelandic refsa, Dutch berispen, Old English refsan.
Inherited from Old Swedish rænnil, from Proto-Germanic *runilaz. Related to ränna (“flow”). See also origin of rinna.

parole.significato: a dish; a specific type of prepared food
parole.testo: From Proto-Germanic *rehtą (“right, law”), related to Etymology 1.

parole.significato: a long, natural crack in the ice cover of the sea or a lake, usually with open (or refrozen) water and more or less wid…
parole.testo: From Proto-Germanic *rēkō. Cognate with Icelandic rák.
Inherited from Old Swedish sēgher, from Proto-Germanic *sīganą. Originally in the sense "dripping slowly".

parole.significato: will, be going to, (except not formal in tone, but a literal match for meaning) shall, is to; (in the past tense "skull…
parole.testo: Apocopic form of skall (“shall”), present tense of skola (see there for additional senses and examples), from Old Norse skulu, from Proto-Germanic *skulaną. Compare senses of Old English sculan.

Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skankô, whence English shank and Norwegian Nynorsk skank. First attested in 1635. The noun is based on an older adjective (now obsolete) skank, skink (limping, lame on one leg).
Inherited from Old Swedish sken, skin, from Proto-Germanic *skīnaną. Cognate of German Schein, English shine.

parole.significato: shear (to deform because of shearing forces)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish skiūva, from Proto-Germanic *skeubaną. Doublet of skuffa. Cognate of German schieben, English shove.
Inherited from Old Swedish skorver, from Proto-Germanic *skurf-, probably from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”). Likely cognate of English scurf, German Schorf.
Inherited from Old Swedish skof (“push”), from Proto-Germanic *skeubaną. Cognate of English shove. Compare German Schub (“[medical] phase”).
From Old Swedish skofl, from Proto-Germanic *skuflō. Cognate with English shovel, German Schaufel.
From Proto-Germanic *skrakwą.

parole.significato: an attic, a loft, a hayloft; an open space immediately beneath the roof of a (farm) building
parole.testo: Possibly related to skull and skalle (“cranium”) (eventually from Proto-Germanic *skallô; compare *skaljō (“husk, shell”)), or a shared origin with Latin celsus (“lofty, high, tall”).

parole.significato: dim (somewhat dark – often with negative connotations)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish skum, from Proto-Germanic *skūmaz. Possibly via Middle Low German schūm, cognate of German Schaum. Compare Dutch schuim, English scum.

parole.significato: bell (carried by animals around their necks)
parole.testo: From Proto-Germanic *skellǭ. If not inherited through Old Norse, borrowed from Middle Low German schelle. Cognate with German Schelle (“small bell”). Related with the verb below.

parole.significato: sharpness; the cutting ability of an edge
parole.testo: From Old Swedish skærpa, from Proto-Germanic *skarpaz (literally “cutting”). A derivative of skarp.

parole.significato: to rinse; to wash with only water
parole.testo: From Old Swedish skylia, from Proto-Germanic *skuljan (alternative form for *skulōn), closely related to Swedish skula.

parole.significato: to slip so as to (nearly) have an accident or other undesirable outcome
parole.testo: From Proto-Germanic *slintanan, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃sleydʰ- (“to slip, slide; to be slippery, slick”).

Inherited from Old Swedish snīkin, from Proto-Germanic *snīkaną. Related to snika and English sneak. Despite superficially having the form of a past participle, originally it was rather suffixed with an adjectival ending meaning "inclined to". Compare with the adjectives fiken, riven, sticken.
From Old Swedish snoor m, an early Old Swedish lengthened form of a snor; like Norwegian snørr and Old Danish snor and snør, from Proto-Germanic *snuza-. Related to snusa.
From Old Swedish snæria, from Proto-Germanic *snarhǭ. See also snara, snår, snörpa.

parole.significato: a spear, a javelin (long stick with a sharp tip)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish spiūt, from Proto-Germanic *speutą. Compare Old Icelandic spjót.

parole.significato: to push back, to resist (literally or figuratively)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish spiærna, from Proto-Germanic *spurnaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sperH-.

parole.significato: plaice; any fish in the genus Pleuronectes; especially species Pleuronectes platessa.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish spotta, from Proto-Germanic *spuþþōną.

From Old Swedish spædher, from Proto-Germanic *spaþja- or Proto-Germanic *spadja-. Probably originally in the meaning of "thin" or "extended in length," therefore ultimately from the root of spänna (“to pull, tighten, span, stretch thin”). Cognate with Danish spæd.

parole.significato: to stem (from), to originate (from), to lead one's ancestry (from)
parole.testo: From Swedish stam (“stem”), from Proto-Germanic *stamniz. Compare with English stem and German stammen.

parole.significato: a frame, a structure ((internal, sturdy) core support structure, of a building, vehicle, vessel, or the like)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish stomme, from Proto-Germanic *stōmô (“stature”), cognate with Gothic 𐍃𐍄𐍉𐌼𐌰 (stōma, “just cause”).

parole.significato: to cut up (usually a slaughtered animal)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish stykkia, from Proto-Germanic *stukkiją. Cognate of Danish stykke.
From Proto-Germanic *stultijǭ. Cognate with English stilt, German Stelze.
From Old Swedish styld, from Proto-Germanic *stuldiz. Compare Old Norse stuldr, which does not have the umlaut.
From Proto-Germanic *sugō; compare Dutch zeug, Low German Söög, West Frisian sûch, English sow, Norwegian sugge; compare also Faroese súgv. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *suh₂kéh₂, from *sū-.

From the neuter form of Old Swedish sälsyn, siäldsyn, siälsyn, siälffsyn. Compound of two parts. The first part is the same root as in sällan and sällsam, from Proto-Germanic *seldanē. The second part is -synt. Thus, literally, "seldom seen".
From Old Swedish sundr, from Proto-Germanic *sundraz, from Proto-Indo-European *sn̥Hter-.

Uncertain. From a surface analysis, a variation of tappa (“to lose, to drop”) (cf. Scanian taba, Danish tabe) in certain situations, either directly or by influence; compare: att tabba det (“to goof up”) vs att tappa det (“to lose the situation”). Other relations are found in words deriving from Pro
Uncertain, but possibly related to tipp (“tip, edge”), similar to Danish tippe and English tip (sense 2). If so, ultimately from a derivative of Proto-Germanic *tuppaz (“top”).
From Old Swedish þrætighi, from Proto-Germanic *þrīz tigiwiz (“thirty”, literally “three tens”); later reformed after tre + tio.

parole.significato: quiet, silent (making or with no or little sound)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish þyster, from Proto-Germanic *þusiþaz. Cognate with Sanskrit तूष्णीम् (tūṣṇī́m, “silent”) and Russian тихий (tíxij, “quiet”).
From Old Swedish tugh, togh, from Proto-Germanic *taugō.

parole.significato: calf; the back side of the lower part of the leg.
parole.testo: Shortening (ca. 1800) of earlier vada (comparable to färg from färga). Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *waþwô. The form may to some degree continue Old Swedish vaþve, from Old Norse vǫðvi, but was probably influenced by cognate Middle Low German wāde and/or modern German Wade.
From Old Swedish valnut, from Proto-Germanic *walhaz (“foreigner”) + Proto-Germanic *hnuts (“nut”). Cognate with Dutch walnoot, German Walnuss, English walnut, Icelandic valhneta.
From Old Swedish vas, from Proto-Germanic *wassaz, possibly derived from Proto-Indo-European *wed- (“water, wet”).

From the oblique case of Old Swedish vissa f (“knowledge, confirmation, assurance”, noun), from Proto-Germanic *gawissaz or Proto-Germanic *wissį̄. Related to viss (“sure”), visserligen (“surely, granted”), visshet (“certainty”), and German wissen (“to know”).
From Old Swedish vitia, from Proto-Germanic *witją, from Proto-Indo-European *weyd-. Doublet of veta.

parole.significato: an (often cramped and secluded) corner of a room or other space
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish vrā, from Proto-Germanic *wranhō. Doublet of vrång.

parole.significato: regale (provide hospitality and supply with food and drink)
parole.testo: väl + fägna, the second part of compound from Proto-Germanic *faginōną.

parole.significato: to (cause to) switch, to (cause to) change (between more-or-less discrete things)
parole.testo: From Proto-Germanic *wihslōną, equivalent to växel + -a.
From ut, from út, from Proto-Germanic *ūt (“out, outward”). Compare Norwegian Bokmål yte (“surface”)
